ann_113.original: The direct edges form a linear score (the long weighted sum is attached as the formula). Through their own edges, capital gains (-2.79 per sd), education level (-1.41), being married to a civilian spouse (-0.73), being a husband (-0.56) or a wife (-0.56), being a man (-0.42), hours per week (-0.33) and capital losses (-0.30) lower the predicted chance of a low income, while living as a child of the household (0.43) and working in other service (0.29) raise it. Self-probe (typical person, whole model): raising the education level from 9 on the 1-16 scale to 13 on the 1-16 scale lowers the predicted chance of a low income from 74% to 24%, and a typical woman gets 87% against 74% for a man, as the direct weights predict. Switching the direct part off (held at its training mean) lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.748.
ann_113.proposed: A weighted sum of every input except age: more education lowers the predicted chance of a low income in stages (from about 89% to about 24% for a typical person), capital gains and losses lower it steadily, and being a woman or not married to a civilian spouse raises it (to about 99% and 97%).

ann_114.original: The model adds to the score for a low income for young people, more the younger they are, and nothing extra above a threshold age. The inner gate is open for every person aged 34 years or younger and for no one older (0 rows at or below that age have it closed and 0 rows above it have it open); that is 16819 of 39073 training rows. For those rows the part adds 0.98 to the score on average compared with switching it off; older people get -0.43, because the switched-off part keeps its always-on unit at its training mean. Self-probe (typical person, whole model): the predicted chance of a low income falls from 98% at 17 years to 82% at 32 years and is 74% at 37 years and at 77 years; it is 76% at 34 years and 74% at 35 years. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.900.
ann_114.proposed: Age lowers the predicted chance of a low income steadily up to about 35 years, then no further (from about 96% at 22 years to about 74% at 58 years for a typical person).

ann_115.original: Above a threshold of capital gains the model lowers the predicted chance of a low income further, on top of the direct capital-gains term. For the typical person the hinge opens between 5200 US dollars and 5300 US dollars; it is open for 1757 training rows, whose outcome rate is 6.1%, and for them it adds -6.29 to the score on average through this part, beside the direct term of -2.79 per sd. ann_121.original: The output adds the direct linear score and the gate contributions on the logit scale and passes the sum through a sigmoid, giving the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less). Because the parts add on the logit scale, a capital gain moves the score by a matching amount at the two ages probed but moves the predicted chance by different amounts. parts.name: income_model_root
parts.original_hypothesis: The output adds the direct linear score and the gate contributions on the logit scale and passes the sum through a sigmoid, giving the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less). The direct linear part carries most of the ranking, and the young-age part and the capital-gain hinge are the next largest by ablation: switching each off lowers the training AUC from 0.9078 to 0.7484, 0.9002 and 0.9067 respectively. Over the 39073 training rows the mean predicted chance is 75.5% against an outcome rate of 76.1%. Because the parts add on the logit scale, a capital gain moves the score by a matching amount at the two ages probed but moves the predicted chance by different amounts. Self-probe (typical person): at 22 years the score is 3.10 with no capital gains and -2.47 with 10000 US dollars; at 45 years it is 1.03 and -4.54, while the predicted chance falls from 96% to 8% for the younger person and from 74% to 1% for the older. The annotated model reproduces the original to within 5.0e-16 on the training rows.
